We learn from the Mississippian, of the 18th,

that the following resolution, providing for the appointment, by the Mississippi Legislature, of Commissioner with authority to proceed to Virginia, to consult with reference to the matters therein set forth, was introduced in the Senate of Mississippi, on the 18th, by Mr. Starke, of Bolivar:

"Resolved by the Senate (the House concurring,) That the Legislature will, at an early day, elect Commissioner to go immediately to Virginia, to confer with her, through her own Legislature, as to the best means to maintain and preserve the rights and interests of the Southern States, against the dangers now impending over them."

We shall welcome a Commissioner from Mississippi to Virginia, should one be appointed, with all hospitality and with fraternal salutations. We have no objection to hearing announced the views, wishes and purposes of our sister Southern States, on the great question and issue between the two sections of this country. The apprehension that the leading object and desire of several of our Southern sister States, is dissolution of the Union, at the earliest possible moment, is real. And if so, we have only to say, so far as we are concerned, that we have no sympathy with such object, and entertain no such desire at the present time. We are ready and willing to go with those who go farthest, in any just and rational measures for the protection and defense of Southern rights and interests. But we are neither ready nor willing to appeal to that last resort—a dissolution of the Union—on account of any aggression or pretended aggression of the North, down to the present hour.—Richmond Wing.

The Wing is assured that the resolution above quoted was moved by a leading member of its own party, who was identified with what was known as the Union organization in 1851. With the exception of the insignificant faction whose trumpeter is the author of the so-called Opposition address, public sentiment in Mississippi is unanimous in favor of providing measures for the protection of the South against the dangers now impending over her. A small party, with Mr. Lake (the late Opposition candidate for Congress in this District) at their head, propose a Convention of all the States that new guarantees for the security of the South may be provided, or peaceful separation effected; while the great body of the people, as represented in the legislature, rely upon the cooperation and concurrent action of the slave holding States. These last do not object to the proposed General Convention, except for the reason that it will necessarily postpone action until after the Inauguration of the next President who may possibly be of the Black Republican party; and they are not willing to place their trust upon a mode of securing protection which depends upon the sense of justice of the very States which have perpetrated the wrongs complained of and are threatening the prosecution of hostilities in a still more offensive form.

Our Richmond cotemporary need not fear that there is purpose in Mississippi to dissolve the Union on account of any aggression, down to the present hour. These aggressions have been excessive, it is true; but they have been patiently borne, in the eagerness of our people to perpetuate the Union and their willingness to endure long and to suffer much, before dissolving their relations with the Northern States. But the wrongs of the past have taught a lesson which it were madness to disregard. They have taught our people that it is their duty to prepare for future aggressions, the last and crowning of which, and more serious than all others in its nature, would be the election of President upon the single idea of destruction to Southern Institutions. The rapid growth of the organization which proclaims this to be its object, warns us to begin the work of preparation, and to bring about concord of action among the States which have common destiny and are threatened with common ruin.

Unless the Wing is willing to deny that we have correctly described the aims of the Black Republican organization, and is willing to dispute its unparalleled increase of strength, as illustrated by popular utterances at the polls in the Northern States—it will not hesitate to join in the movement which Mississippi has proposed. If it will not join this movement, it must lag behind, and consent to follow in the rear of the grand army of patriots who are moving forward with one heart and one resolute purpose to preserve unimpaired, and to transmit to posterity, the rights for which their fathers fought.

The Ideal.


The Ideal is the Heaven of the soul. De-
sire would end with its obtainment, and
every longing would be satisfied.


The Ideal alone is beautiful; for with all
else there is the stain of Earth, the dross of
mixed mortality.


If there be reason for belief in our own
deathlessness, it lies within the constant con-
sciousness of the Ideal, which glimmers star
like, from above, through all the night of
circumstance and time.


The spirit sees in the Ideal all its posi-
